Reimagining the university for a more sustainable world
Karen MacGregor  03 July  2025
Tweet“The greatest potential of the Sustainable Development Goals framework is to help us reimagine what the university does. The big risk is the SDGs’ superficial adoption by higher education,” Harvard University education professor Fernando Reimers told last week’s “Time to Act” University World News-ABET webinar.
“The SDGs are a very generative framework to support synergies across the three elements of the mission of the university – teaching, research and extension – as well as collaborations, both within the university community and across university communities,” he said.
“In effect, they provide a common language,” he told the 26 June webinar titled “Time to Act: Embedding Sustainability in Higher Education”.
This article is part of a series on Education for Sustainable Development published by University World News in partnership with ABET. University World News is solely responsible for the editorial content.
But if universities respond to the SDGs as an additional rather than an essential project: “This would translate into either something siloed, disconnected from the very core missions of the university, or would translate into an initiative that would affect a limited number of students.”
The webinar
Reimers, Ford Foundation Professor of the Practice of International Education at the Harvard Graduate School of Education, was one of four high-level experts on the panel.
Dr Debra Rowe is president of the US Partnership for Education for Sustainable Development and a leader within the global Higher Education Sustainability Initiative (HESI), a partnership between 10 United Nations entities and the global higher education community.
She is excited by growing interest in and activity around educating for sustainability. “What is key now is to take your solutions and not just keep them local; scale them up so we can get to a higher level of implementation.”
Ratna Lindawati Lubis, a professor of economics and business at Telkom University, Indonesia, is also a fellow of HESI’s SDG Publishers Compact Fellows group.
Technology and masses of free sustainability resources are enabling students and academics in the Global South to bridge the gap with the north, she said: “But the first question is the commitment. Are you ready?”
Dr Michael Milligan is CEO of ABET, the global non-profit quality assurance agency that is leading in integrating sustainability knowledge, skills and awareness into accreditation standards for the nearly 5,000 STEM programmes in 42 countries that it accredits and which graduate more than 200,000 students annually.
“Incorporating sustainability isn’t a burden – it’s a necessity,” Milligan told the webinar. “Change is never easy, but in this case, we don’t have a choice. Our futures depend on it.”
The webinar was the third in an ongoing webinar series with University World News and ABET. The series is exploring issues of great importance to higher education and society in times of uncertainty.
“I think we can all agree that we’re in one of those times,” said webinar moderator Brendan O’Malley, editor-in-chief of University World News.
The webinar drew 300 participants from around the world, including university leaders (11%), senior academics (24%), academics (16%), administrators (17%) and students (14%), among others.
Audience polls reflected challenges and priorities in embedding sustainability into higher education that were also raised by the panellists. People could select several options.
The top barriers identified were lack of staff training or awareness (55%), curriculum overload or limited space for new content (44%), and weak institutional leadership or policy support (41%). Also highlighted were funding constraints (38%), resistance to change or institutional inertia (35%) and the perception that sustainability is not relevant across all disciplines (24%).
When asked about institutional priorities for integrating the SDGs, the most common response was greening campus operations (48%), then whole-institution, multifaceted approaches (42%), curriculum development (40%) and community engagement (39%).
And what about the support needed? Over half (51%) cited professional development and training. Other helpful measures included cross-disciplinary collaboration (43%), leadership mandates or strategic prioritisation (42%), and access to case studies and teaching resources (41%).
Multiple ways to relate education to the SDGs
Reimers founded and leads the Global Education Innovation Initiative and is an expert on education policy, global education, and more laterally on sustainability. He is a good example of how it is possible to connect with the SDGs in multiple ways.
For instance, Reimers was on the UNESCO panel that produced the 2021 UNESCO report on the Futures of Education, which “gives universities a seminal role in advancing the 2030 agenda”.
Further, “All my teaching is basically about supporting my students to develop competencies that can help them advance not only SDG 4, the education goal, but all the SDGs.” This is often done through project-based courses in which students work with authorities on educational challenges, using the SDGs as a framework.
Reimers’ research is on using the SDGs as part of strategies for innovation. One recent paper was on how the SDGs can be used as a framework to stimulate innovation in higher education. At Harvard, he served on the task force that developed a climate action plan for the institution.
“In my own work, advising universities, my focus is very much on how do we make universities more socially embedded, more relevant to the needs of society? I find the SDGs are a very useful framework to advance those conversations.”
Lastly, Reimers has designed with collaborators an entire curriculum aligned with the SDGs that extends from kindergarten upwards and has been used by a number of universities.
In a recent paper, Reimers examined different approaches by universities in educating students for climate action. One exemplary institution was the Monterey Institute of Technology in Mexico, which looks for ways to align everything in research and teaching with the SDGs.
That is how Reimers used the SDGs in building curricula. “It’s not about teaching the SDGs as content.
It’s about translating the SDGs into a set of competencies that students should have so that they understand them, they care about them, and most importantly, they have some skills to make some difference with respect to poverty alleviation, sustainability and so on,” he noted.
Lots happening, more needed
The webinar offered a range of approaches and practices involving education for sustainability. It underscored the vast amount of activity underway and the increasing widespread acceptance of Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) – across higher education and its stakeholders.
For 20 years, the US Partnership for Education for Sustainable Development that Rowe leads has had networks of associations. One is the Disciplinary Associations Network for Sustainability, which has dozens of academic societies that work on integrating sustainability into curricula.
There are a myriad of free resources supporting ESD.
Rowe provides a taste with her resource list. She also pointed to the University World News SDGs hub and the EPIC network for project models and community engagement tools.
Further, Rowe highlighted STARS – the Sustainability Tracking, Assessment and Rating System, which enables universities to assess their sustainability efforts and gauge progress; it has more than 13,000 resources.
“We find that there are a lot of wonderful resources out there, but those resources don't always get followed up with support communities,” said Debra Rowe.
To help solve this problem, Rowe unveiled a new Community of Support – Integrating Sustainability into Higher Education and Society at the webinar. It is an initiative involving the two HESI action groups Rowe chairs, Education for Green Jobs and the SDGs Publishers Compact Fellows, and University World News.
Click here to join.
More than 200 publishing companies are signed up with the HESI publishers’ group. Right after the webinar, Rowe met with one of the world’s major educational publishers, which is interested in integrating sustainability into textbooks across its disciplines.
For Rowe, one of the many ways of educating for sustainability starts with this theme: How can we use what we’re learning to make the world a better place?
“When you set that question up at the beginning of a programme and keep it all the way through, it activates students to really care, instead of sitting around in doom and gloom.
“The best education is real-world problem-solving,” she continued.
“Students see that learning is important, not only for their careers and all their adult roles but also in being able to contribute to a better world. We’ve seen this come alive in disadvantaged communities as well as in privileged communities, as we’ve used this theme.”
Rowe stressed that all disciplines have an important role to play in sustainability. “We see the hard sciences, doing climate science, for example, saying: ‘Please bring in our social scientists so we can get into the behaviour changes that we need.’”
Some challenges
The webinar poll showed that people have problems with curriculum overload. But Rowe and Milligan argued that no additional curriculum space is required when integrating sustainability into teaching and learning.
Rowe has a five-minute exercise. “I say to educators, take a concept you have to teach anyway in your course, and now take a sustainability concept. Explain how you’re going to teach both at the same time. At first, it’s the deer-in-the-headlights look. But within minutes, they are engaged and the room erupts with examples.
“Educators are worried about the future. They want to be more relevant. They want to make their courses interesting to students, beyond those that are just dedicated to the subject. Bringing in sustainability really helps,” she stated.
What about internal resistance? Rowe knows this is a problem. However, “once you show doubters that this is an international trend and actually it could be more harmful if they don’t get on board, it tends to help faculty move in the sustainability direction”, she noted.
Regarding curriculum overload, Michael Milligan said true integration is both possible and essential. He recommended the Engineering for One Planet toolkit as an excellent free resource. The toolkit has mapped ABET accreditation criteria to sustainability activities that are easily integrated into curricula.
He also spoke of concerns that adding sustainability could “stifle innovation. That couldn’t be further from the truth.” There are very many accredited programmes that are successfully preparing graduates who are technically skilled and socially conscious and innovative.
Indonesia: Entrepreneurial thinking and technology
Ratna Lubis has had a more than 25-year academic career and is an expert in entrepreneurship education and strategic management. She highlighted the importance of leadership and of role models in scaling up sustainability efforts.
Since 2017, blown away by the SDGs, Lubis has led students in her master’s in management programme on project-based learning involving upcycling with the community. She has also collaborated with the University of Bergen in Norway on SDG-related initiatives, connecting classroom learning with the real world.
Drawing on her doctoral research, she introduced a learning model for entrepreneurship leadership that is rooted in Indonesia’s rich cultural diversity, which she sees as key to global engagement and problem-solving around sustainable development.
She told the webinar that the COVID-19 pandemic had helped to familiarise students in Indonesia and elsewhere with project- and case-based learning using resources from the internet.
“Students align projects with the SDGs they care about – like SDG 4 for early childhood education or SDG 12 for upcycling project-based learning,” she said. “They chose which SDG, which they love doing.”
Her business ethics classes explore SDGs 8 for economic growth, 12 for responsible consumption, and 17 for partnerships. “I choose a case-based assignment, and the student uses free resources from the internet and is happy doing that.”
Technology and social media, including YouTube, are used to showcase student work. Lubis encourages her students to draw on free global sustainability resources.
Asked about sustainability constraints on universities in the Global South, Lubis said new technology provides one solution, enabling people and universities to connect with those in the Global North. “We have a gap because now, by using technology, we can have a conversation.”
It is important to share failures and hope: “It is lonely when I feel I’m the only one doing this sustainability thing. But then when I connect and join the conversation, I feel there is hope for all of us.” Big challenges include the time differences and the language barrier – although again, AI-supported translation tools are helping.
A role for policy
There is an important role for policy in supporting education for sustainability, and Reimers talked about both institutional and public policies.
“At the institutional level, strategies that embed the SDGs into the process of strategic planning create an enabling environment that makes it possible for universities to become more socially embedded,” he said.
And they do – this was shown by a global study of universities during the pandemic. “When sustainability is an objective, it makes it possible for people to collaborate.”
Turning to public policy, Reimers said there were positive policies and negative policies.
He cited South Korea’s alignment of universities with regional strategies as a model of positive policy, in contrast to the United States federal government’s efforts to politicise higher education to conform with its ideological preferences, as are other countries such as Hungary and Turkey.
“Any government that tries to politicise universities and to use their financial support or their norms to get universities to advance a particular political or ideological agenda – it’s going to put the university in a defensive, reactive mode, which is the opposite of being socially embedded.”
“In my own institution, where we have refused to accept the unlawful demands of government to gain control over faculty appointments and student admissions and curriculum, it’s a huge distraction to us.” Work to become more socially embedded goes out the window.
“Policy makes the whole difference, and there are smart policies and there are dumb policies, and we have examples of both around the world.”
Working in partnerships
Michael Milligan spoke about the roles of partnerships in helping to facilitate the integration of sustainability. “I always think about that saying: ‘If you want to go fast, go alone. If you want to go far, go together.’
“The path to a sustainable world is going to be long and complicated. SDG 17 is about partnerships. Without partnerships, we’re not going to make a lot of progress,” Milligan said. ABET has direct agreements with organisations around the world, including with University of World News.
In the engineering field alone, ABET has 26 partners across continents. “This is important because we’ve agreed that when students graduate, they have to have some exposure to various topics, and sustainability is incorporated into all of those worldwide.”
Among others, ABET belongs to the World Federation of Engineering Organisations – which was a key contributor in developing the UN SDGs – the Global Engineering Deans Council, and the International Federation of Engineering Education Societies.
“But equally important, maybe even more important, is the bottom-up approach,” said Milligan, citing Engineering For One Planet and the grassroots efforts of faculty and students.
Rowe highlighted networks of universities in the Global South, such as ProSPER.Net, a UN-based alliance of 55 Asia Pacific universities advancing sustainability in postgraduate education.
The importance of leadership
Major disruptions around the world are challenging universities, and there is system-wide higher education transformation underway,” said Reimers.
“There’s a way in which leadership can steer that transformation towards a world that is more inclusive, in which we relate to each other in peaceful ways, and in which we relate to the planet in a way that is sustainable.
“What we need is leadership that can look beyond the immediate present and the challenges, leadership that has a well-developed and informed vision but also courage and humility to respond to that vision, to communicate it, and to do it in a way that engages others.
“There are already examples in every institution of social embeddedness in which the SDGs are used to help transform the university. One of the things that leadership can do is take the time to learn what is happening in the institution, spotlight that, ask how to support it, amplify it and then challenge others in the university community to follow suit.
“But I have no illusions,” Reimers told the webinar. “This is a ‘blood, toil, tears and sweat’ moment, to use the words of Winston Churchill.
At least in my institution, given the attacks by the administration of President Trump, we’re all clear that for the next four years, every day is going to be more challenging than the last day and less challenging than the next day.”
Adding to the leadership discussion, from another angle, Rowe said her organisations sometimes contact university leaders to let them know that there is a great sustainability initiative on campus that they would like to profile and that this would amplify the university’s profile. That helps to make presidents aware of the positive possibilities of sustainability initiatives.
“We also work with associations,” such as the International Association of Universities, and active networks around the world, she stated.
“The association level is the next level up and is where heads of universities go.” If they hear about the importance of sustainability, “it tends to build support.
“What’s urgent is for us all to think on the systems level and to leverage points for systemic change to shift norms and policies,” Rowe stressed.
During questions, Michael Milligan spoke about the critical role of leadership buy-in. He cited King’s College, London, which adopted at the highest level an institutional commitment to a sustainable campus and programmes – everything from dining halls to across curricula.
“They see this as necessary and as what students need to be exposed to. Living sustainability as well as learning it makes a huge difference.”
Final takeaway
In today’s geopolitical environment, Milligan concluded, it is crucial to maintain momentum on educating for sustainability. “The biggest takeaway from our discussion is that we are making progress. Unfortunately, time’s not on our side.
“We have to attack problems in a very thoughtful and direct way. It is critically important to make sure that we feel tomorrow will be better than today and that these problems are solvable.
The solutions to many of today’s challenges are known, but often people impede progress. Getting people to think longer-term is probably one of the biggest challenges for sustainability.
“On the very positive side, our greatest asset is the students coming out of our sustainability programmes,” Milligan continued, and he too stressed the important role of entrepreneurship.
“Students will have many opportunities as they enter the workforce to come up with novel ideas about how to attack certain problems and with the entrepreneurial spirit to develop solutions that can make a difference.
“Part of what we want to do, in integrating sustainability topics in the STEM fields, is to drive that entrepreneurial spirit,” he concluded.

Harvard fights back as antisemitism battle escalates
Nathan M Greenfield  04 July  2025
TweetThe Trump administration significantly escalated its battle with Harvard University over how it addressed antisemitism on Monday, formally accusing the university of violating federal civil rights law and threatening immediate withdrawal of funding. But Harvard immediately pushed back via a revised filing to the Federal Court.
On 30 June, the Office of Civil Rights (OCR) of the Health and Human Services Department issued a Notice of Violation (NoV) letter declaring that Harvard violated Title VI of the Civil Rights Act (CRA, 1965) by being “in some cases deliberately indifferent” and in others “a wilful participant in antisemitic harassment of Jewish students, faculty, and staff”, especially during the pro-Palestinian protests following the start of the Israel-Hamas war.
After being served a NoV declaring that Harvard violated Title VI of the Civil Rights Act, the university filed papers in the Federal Court stating that “us[ing] the power of the State to punish or suppress” academic decisions the government opposes is “presumptively unconstitutional”.
Harvard’s lawyers reworked a brief scheduled to be filed that afternoon asking the Federal Court to vacate earlier government orders freezing US$2.6 billion of research grants.
The additions to the filing argue that the government violated Title VI’s administrative requirements and that it erred by relying on Harvard’s own report on antisemitism instead of conducting its own investigation.
The NoV is a significant escalation in the Trump administration’s battle with Harvard, as it asserts: “Failure to institute adequate changes immediately will result in the loss of all federal financial resources.”
Just ten days earlier, amidst a number of articles in the media about behind-the-scenes negotiations between Harvard and the administration, President Donald J Trump posted on Truth Social, ending with his trademark use of capital letters: “We have been working closely with Harvard, and it is very possible that a Deal will be announced over the next week or so.
They have acted extremely appropriately during these negotiations, and appear to be committed to doing what is right. If a Settlement is made on the basis that is currently being discussed, it will be ‘mindbogglingly’ HISTORIC.”
JTFCA vs ATFR antisemitism reports
The NoV letter and the 57-page report accompanying it were issued by the Joint Task Force to Combat Anti-Semitism (JTFCA) that combined officials from the Department of Justice, Department of Education, Department of Health and Human Services, and the General Services Administration (which administers grants).
Struck on 3 February, the JTFCA was tasked with determining if, by failing to protect Jewish students from antisemitism, Harvard had violated Title VI of the CRA, which “prohibits discrimination on the basis of race, colour, and national origin” in federally funded agencies or institutions that receive federal financial assistance.
Basing itself on Harvard’s Antisemitism Task Force Report (ATFR) published on 29 April, the JTFCA reported that almost 60% of Jewish students surveyed reported experiencing “discrimination, stereotyping, or negative bias on campus due to [their] views on current events” [that is, Hamas’ attack on Israel on 7 October 2022 and Israel’s subsequent war against Hamas in Gaza].
The JTFCA also accepted the ATFR’s findings that “26 per cent of Jewish students surveyed reported feeling physically unsafe, and 44 per cent reported feeling mentally unsafe [at Harvard]. More than two-thirds of Jewish students “expressed discomfort sharing their opinions in general”, while 73% felt that way about expressing their political opinions.
(The ATFR also reported that Muslims too found Harvard’s leafy campus in Cambridge, Massachusetts baleful: 47% of Muslim students surveyed indicated that they feel physically unsafe on campus, and 61% feel mentally unsafe, information the JTFCA ignored in its report.)
What is Harvard’s culpability?
The JTFCA report lists numerous examples of antisemitic acts recorded by Harvard’s ATFR, among them, a Jew wearing a yarmulke being spat on, Orthodox Jews being told to hide their kippahs under baseball hats and being jeered at with calls including shouts of “Heil Hitler!”
On Sidechat, a social media platform limited to students with Harvard email addresses, calls to ‘gas all the Jews’ and ‘let ‘em cook’ received upvotes. Student and faculty groups posted Instagram cartoons that included the Star of David, dollar signs, and nooses.
The JTFCA quotes the ATFR saying that “some Jewish students were informed by their peers, teaching fellows, and even in some cases, faculty, that they were associated with something offensive and, in some cases, that their very presence was offensive.”
The JTFCA declared Harvard’s institutional responses, including a compliance review of Harvard Medical School’s commencement ceremony, which was accused of being antisemitic, and the placing of the Palestine Solidarity campaign on probation, “too little, too late”.
The government investigators were also dismissive of Harvard’s replacement of the leadership of the Center for Middle Eastern Studies and the two years it has taken to incorporate “antisemitism and anti-Israel bias” into university training sessions.
Since the above incidents were reported by Harvard itself, whether they occurred or not is not the legal question at the heart of the NoV. What is Harvard’s culpability?
Accordingly, the government asserts that Harvard “had ‘actual knowledge’ of the harassment for the purposes of Title VI liability”, as demonstrated by the fact that on 27 October 2023 (that is, three weeks after Hamas’ attack on Israel and ten days after Israel invaded Gaza), “Harvard University announced the formation of an Anti-Semitism Advisory Group.”
Three weeks later, campus police restricted access to certain buildings. In December, Harvard’s then president, Claudine Gay, testified before Congress on antisemitism on campus.
Further, the JTFCA asserts: “Harvard exercised substantial control over the harassment and discrimination that Jewish and Israeli students experienced,” though not because America’s oldest and most prestigious university coordinated it.
Rather, the government bases this argument on a 1999 decision of the Supreme Court of the United States (SCOTUS) in which it ruled that an education institution “exercises substantial control over both the harasser and the context in which the known harassment occurs” when it “occurs during school hours on school grounds.”
In essence, the argument is that Harvard is culpable because it did not stop the harassment by using its powers to control its property, remove persons who are harassing others and prevent them from enjoying access to all campus facilities.
The government also cites a 2003 case involving the State University of New York, in which the state court ruled that “institutions can be found to be deliberately indifferent to discrimination ‘when remedial action only follows after a lengthy and unjustifiable delay’”, as support for its claim that Harvard’s slowness in acting against antisemitism amounts to discrimination.
First Amendment rights
In their filing in the Federal Court on Monday, Harvard’s lawyers ignored almost all of the government’s arguments and focused attention on the university’s First Amendment rights and the government’s ignoring of both the mechanisms Title VI lays out for an NoV to be issued and the government’s refusal to follow the regulations laid out in the Administrative Procedures Act (APA), which covers how grants are to be monitored and, if necessary, withdrawn.
The government agrees that Harvard enjoys First Amendment protections.
Yet, at the same time, the government “does not dispute that its mandatory conditions [for example, turning over student disciplinary records] and retaliatory actions [to continue receiving federal funds] are viewpoint based”, write Harvard’s lawyers; citing a 2024 (SCOTUS) decision that found for the National Rifle Association, the lawyers told the court that “‘us[ing] the power of the State to punish or suppress’ Harvard’s ‘disfavoured expression’ [including academic decisions the government opposes] is ‘presumptively unconstitutional’.”
Harvard’s lawyers mounted the similar arguments against an entirely new legal theory proffered by the government, “that Harvard’s First Amendment rights ‘are circumscribed’ because Harvard is a government ‘contractor’.”
Additionally, while the government asserted its actions against Harvard were solely because of the university’s violation of Title VI and its failure to protect Jewish students, Harvard’s lawyers adduced numerous examples of administration officials saying that they were acting against Harvard because it lacked “viewpoint diversity”.
Secretary of Education Linda McMahon’s letter of 5 May, for example, criticised Harvard for being “left-leaning” and opposed to free markets.
The lawyers concluded this part of their brief by quoting Trump saying that “every time [Harvard] fight, they lose another $250 million.”
Trump administration’s ‘authoritarian desires’
Harvard’s arguments that the Trump administration was violating both Title VI and the APA are broadly similar. Even though the government claims that its actions against Harvard are underwritten by the fact that Harvard violated Title VI’s provisions against discrimination, Harvard’s lawyers argue, the government has not followed the investigative procedures mandated by Title VI and the APA into events on Harvard’s campus.
“The administrative record does not document any meaningful investigation by the Government into antisemitism on Harvard’s campus,” the brief states, before continuing: “Nor does it identify any specific incidents of such conduct [from its own research], let alone connect such incidents to any terminated grants.”
In other words, the incidents the JTFCA pulls from Harvard’s report have no relation to the grants, either for medical [and] health or defence research.
“The most the Government can do is repeatedly cite Harvard’s own Task Force report.” And, equally importantly, since this “report was released two weeks after the Government froze all research funds to Harvard”, it could not “possibly have been the basis for the challenged actions”.
In other words, the Trump administration is engaged in post hoc reasoning in regard to the legal warrant for its actions against Harvard, which is illegal. Harvard’s lawyers go on to point out that the report itself undercuts the government’s claim that Harvard was dismissive of the complaints by Jewish students.
“The fact that Trump gutted Harvard’s funding first, before an investigation, is evidence that these actions are purely political. The goal of this notice is to punish Harvard for standing up against the administration.
The end goal is to make all academic institutions capitulate to this administration’s authoritarian desires,” wrote Isaac Kamola, professor of political science at Trinity College (Hartford, Connecticut) and director of the Center for the Defense of Academic Freedom, in an email to University World News.
A central part of Harvard’s brief argues against the Government’s claim that it has the inherent power to cancel contracts; the APA lays out the investigative procedures that must be followed to cancel contracts at “agency discretion”, which the Trump administration asserts boils down to government policy.
While discussing the requirements under the APA, the Harvard lawyers write, the Government “does not identify any document in the administrative record [of Harvard] where an agency analysed and weighed evidence to reasonably conclude that Harvard has failed to ‘take adequate actions to prevent antisemitism’.”
The lack of the proverbial “smoking gun” leads the government, Harvard’s lawyers assert, to fall back on the fact that at times the officials responsible for the APA have “accept[ed] explanations ‘of less than ideal clarity’”.
Harvard’s lawyers respond to this fact by stating baldly: “The APA may sometimes be forgiving, but it is not standardless.”
“The Government cannot simply proclaim that it was acting to combat antisemitism without pointing to any record evidence [from its own investigation], without explaining why Harvard’s myriad of actions addressing antisemitism are insufficient, without considering whether any legitimate concerns about antisemitism could be addressed through less drastic actions.”
As for the Trump administration’s claim that it is fighting antisemitism, Kamola was having none of it. “Let’s be clear. The Trump administration does not care about addressing antisemitism. Members from this administration have expressed admiration of Hitler and supported Germany’s Nazi Party.
“Trump has surrounded himself with a cadre of proud white nationalists, neo-Nazis, and Holocaust denialists. And his top advisor, Elon Musk, gave a Nazi salute during an inauguration event and faced no consequence for doing so,” he stated.

Public universities to launch foreign-language programmes
Philenews  18 July  2025
TweetParliament has approved legislation allowing public universities in Cyprus to offer undergraduate degree programmes in foreign languages, ending a seven-year legislative delay that university rectors describe as a crucial first step towards internationalisation, reports Evangelia Sizopoulou for Philenews.
The University of Cyprus will be permitted to offer six foreign-language programmes plus two interdisciplinary ones, totalling eight programmes, while the Cyprus University of Technology can provide three foreign-language programmes plus one interdisciplinary programme, totalling four.
University of Cyprus Rector Tasos Christofides said institutions are not ready for immediate implementation, noting required certification procedures through the relevant authority DIPAE must be completed first. Jillian Segal was appointed to the role a year ago in response to a surge in reports of attacks against Jewish sites and property in Australia, following Israel’s invasion of Gaza, and was tasked with combating antisemitism in the country, reports Hilary Whiteman for CNN.
Standing alongside Prime Minister Anthony Albanese Thursday, Segal released a report nine months in the making proposing strong measures, including the university funding threats and the screening of visa applicants for extremist views.
“The plan is not about special treatment for one community; it is about restoring equal treatment,” Segal said. “It’s about ensuring that every Australian, regardless of their background or belief, can live, work, learn and prosper in this country.”

It said the policy, designed to optimise public resource utilisation by restructuring the funding framework, will take effect from 2026, reports Owede Agbajileke for The Guardian Nigeria.
Minister of State for Education, Professor Suwaiba Ahmad, stated this at the 2025 policy meeting in Abuja. Professor Ahmad questioned the fairness of distributing the same amount of resources to schools with low enrolment as to those with much larger student populations. The minister, therefore, urged TETFund beneficiary institutions to exceed the government’s student enrolment benchmark to continue accessing funding from the agency.

Yet when he left the service and tried to apply that expertise toward an education at Pittsburgh’s Community College of Allegheny County (CCAC), he was given just three credits toward a required class in physical education, writes Jon Marcus for The Hechinger Report.

The award is in recognition of NHS Fife’s commitment to education, research and innovation, and acknowledges its partnership with the University of St Andrews. It will officially be known as NHS Fife University Health Board, and was granted the status by the Scottish parliament.
The formal partnership between the health board and the university followed the end of a historic prohibition preventing St Andrews from awarding its own medical qualifications.
